title: Mihin and minne: answering with -lle
summary: Use mihin or minne for a destination in the at/on family too. Mihin sinä menet? — Menen asemalle.
prerequisiteSkills: Mihin and minne: answering with common into-forms
objectives: Ask where to with mihin or minne.
Answer with -lle for the taught destinations and surfaces.

sections.title: Meaning and pattern
paragraphs: Singular refers to one person or one thing in these patterns.
Plural means more than one in this grammatical pattern.
The illative is an into/to form; mihin aikaan uses that form in a time expression.
A weak stem uses the changed consonants shown in the construction steps; the strong stem keeps the corresponding strong consonants.
Use mihin or minne for a destination in the at/on family too. The ending -lle means to or onto: asemalle (“to the station”), pöydälle (“onto the table”). It has no vowel-harmony variant.
keyPoints: Do not choose missä for movement towards the destination.

sections.title: Answering the question
paragraphs: Give the intended destination: Menen asemalle (“I am going to the station”). In placement sentences the destination can be a surface: Laitan kirjan pöydälle (“I am putting the book on the table”). The object and verb forms are provided here.
A natural short reply to “Mihin sinä menet?” is “Asemalle.” (“To the station.”). Use the full reply when it makes the person, action or correction clearer.
A negative correction does not change the destination ending. Reject the wrong destination with the supplied en mene, then give the actual -lle destination.
The exercises show supporting Finnish words and their meanings when recalling them is not the task. Read the complete English meaning before choosing the question or answer form.
keyPoints: Use -lle for these destinations, not -lla/-llä or -lta/-ltä.

sections.title: Build the answer forms
paragraphs: asemalle means to the station here. Asema + -lle gives asemalle; -lle has no vowel-harmony alternative.
torille means to the market square here. Tori + -lle gives torille.
pihalle means into the yard here. Piha + -lle gives pihalle.
pöydälle means onto the table here. Pöytä changes t to d before -lle: pöydälle.
tuolille means onto the chair here. Tuoli + -lle gives tuolille.
keyPoints: Use -lle for these destinations, not -lla/-llä or -lta/-ltä.

steps: Mihin: where to; question asking where to. Mihin is the illative question form; in mihin aikaan it instead asks at what time.
sinä: you; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Sinä addresses one person informally.
menet: you go; verb (the action or state). Mene- + singular second-person -t gives menet.

steps: Menen: I go; verb (the action or state). Mennä removes -nä and adds e to form mene-, then adds -n: menen.

hän: he or she; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Hän refers to one other person without specifying gender.
menee: goes; verb (the action or state). Lengthen the final e of mene-: menee.

examples.english: Where are you putting the bag?
steps: Mihin: where to; question asking where to. Mihin is the illative question form; in mihin aikaan it instead asks at what time.
sinä: you; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Sinä addresses one person informally.
laitat: you put; verb (the action or state). Weak laita- + singular second-person -t gives laitat.
laukun: the bag; object (the thing the action concerns). Laukku changes kk to k before -n: laukun. The complete object form is supplied.

steps: Laitan: I put; verb (the action or state). Laittaa forms weak laita- with tt → t, then adds -n: laitan.

examples.english: I am not going to the station. I am going to the market square.
steps: En: I do not; negative verb (marks not and identifies the person). En is the first-person singular negative verb. The main verb takes its negative form.
mene: go; main verb after the negative verb. Remove -n from menen to obtain negative mene, unchanged after every present negative verb.
